subject: Economy
sub_topic: GDP calculation — expenditure, income, output methods

concepts.name: GDP vs GNP vs NNP: Definitional Boundaries and Interconversion
key_dimensions: Role of Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) in converting GDP to GNP
Role of depreciation (Capital Consumption Allowance) in converting GNP to NNP
Why GNP > GDP for capital-exporting nations and GNP < GDP for capital-importing nations like India
UPSC trap: NNP at market price vs NNP at factor cost (Net National Income)

concepts.name: Market Price vs Factor Cost vs Basic Price: Three Valuation Concepts
key_dimensions: GDP at Market Price = GDP at Basic Price + Net Taxes on Products
GDP at Factor Cost = GDP at Basic Price – Net Production Taxes (older SNA convention)
Why India shifted from Factor Cost to Basic Price as primary measure post-2011 base revision
UPSC trap: 'Basic Price' is NOT the same as 'Factor Cost' — subsidies vs taxes at product level vs production level

concepts.name: Expenditure Method: Components of GDP (C + I + G + NX)
key_dimensions: Precise definitions of Consumption (C), Investment (I), Government Expenditure (G), Net Exports (NX)
UPSC trap: Government Transfer Payments (pensions, subsidies) are NOT included in G
Distinction between Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) and Change in Inventories within Investment
Why exports are added and imports subtracted — avoiding double-counting of foreign-produced goods

concepts.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF): Components and Significance
key_dimensions: Four sub-components: Machinery & Equipment, Construction, Intellectual Property Products, Cultivated Biological Resources
GFCF as a proxy for investment rate — its role in assessing productive capacity of the economy
UPSC trap: Purchase of existing assets (land, second-hand machinery) is NOT part of GFCF
Public vs Private GFCF trends in India and their policy implications

concepts.name: Change in Inventories (Stock-Building) as a GDP Component
key_dimensions: Why unsold goods produced in a period must be counted in GDP — output-expenditure identity
Distinction between planned and unplanned inventory accumulation
UPSC trap: Inventory drawdown (negative change) reduces GDP even if sales are high
Valuation of inventories at current prices vs historical cost — impact on GDP measurement

concepts.name: Income Method: Factor Incomes and Their Classification
key_dimensions: Four factor payments: Compensation of Employees (wages), Gross Operating Surplus (profit/rent/interest), Gross Mixed Income, Net Taxes on Production
UPSC trap: 'Gross Mixed Income' covers self-employed/unincorporated enterprises — crucial for India's large informal sector
Transfer payments (unemployment benefits, pensions) are explicitly excluded — they are not factor incomes
Distinction between Nominal Wages and Real Wages in the context of national income deflation

concepts.name: Output/Value-Added Method: Concept of Value Added and Avoiding Double Counting
key_dimensions: Value Added = Output Value – Intermediate Consumption (not the same as profit)
Why only final goods or value added is counted — the double-counting problem illustrated with wheat→flour→bread
Three-sector breakdown: Agriculture, Industry, Services — India's sectoral GDP composition
UPSC trap: Intermediate goods used in production are excluded; capital goods (investment) are included as final goods

concepts.name: Gross Value Added (GVA) vs GDP: The Bridge Equation
key_dimensions: GDP = GVA at Basic Prices + Taxes on Products – Subsidies on Products
Why GVA is preferred at sector level while GDP is used at aggregate economy level
UPSC trap: Sectoral growth rates in India's National Accounts are reported in GVA terms, not GDP
Implications when taxes on products grow faster than GVA — GDP growth can exceed GVA growth

concepts.name: Real GDP vs Nominal GDP: GDP Deflator and Price Indices
key_dimensions: Nominal GDP uses current year prices; Real GDP uses base year prices — only real GDP reflects actual output growth
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100 — broader than CPI or WPI as it covers all domestically produced goods
UPSC trap: GDP Deflator is NOT a fixed-weight index; its basket changes each year unlike CPI
Difference between GDP Deflator and CPI — CPI includes imports; GDP Deflator excludes imports but includes capital goods

concepts.name: Base Year Revision in National Accounts: India's 2011-12 Base Year
key_dimensions: Why base years are revised — to reflect structural changes in the economy and adopt new SNA 2008 norms
Key changes in India's 2015 revision: shift to market price, inclusion of financial sector profits, new data sources (MCA21)
UPSC trap: The revision significantly raised India's GDP growth estimates, leading to the 'GDP controversy'
Rebasing changes sectoral shares — services sector share may appear to shrink or grow with new base

concepts.name: System of National Accounts (SNA) 2008: Key Norms and India's Compliance
key_dimensions: SNA 2008 treats R&D expenditure and weapons systems as capital formation (GFCF), not intermediate consumption
Inclusion of financial intermediation services indirectly measured (FISIM) in GDP
UPSC trap: SNA 2008 does NOT include illegal activities in standard GDP (unlike some European countries under ESA 2010)
India's partial compliance — areas where MoSPI still deviates from SNA 2008 norms

concepts.name: Treatment of Government Services in GDP Measurement
key_dimensions: Government non-market services have no market price — valued at cost of production (salaries + intermediate consumption + depreciation)
UPSC trap: This means more government hiring automatically raises GDP even without productive output — a measurement limitation
Distinction between government consumption (current expenditure) and government investment (capital expenditure) in GDP
Why defense expenditure on weapons is now treated as GFCF under SNA 2008, not consumption

concepts.name: Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA): Components and India's Position
key_dimensions: NFIA = Compensation earned by residents abroad – Compensation paid to non-residents + Net investment income + Net remittances of workers
UPSC trap: Remittances from NRIs to India are a transfer, NOT factor income — they do NOT enter GDP or GNP through NFIA in standard accounts
India's NFIA is typically negative — more profits repatriated by foreign firms than Indian firms earn abroad
Difference between current account remittances and factor income in Balance of Payments context

concepts.name: Depreciation (Capital Consumption Allowance): Gross vs Net Aggregates
key_dimensions: Net National Product (NNP) = GNP – Depreciation — NNP better reflects sustainable income
UPSC trap: Depreciation in national accounts is 'economic depreciation' (wear and tear of capital), NOT accounting/tax depreciation
Why GDP (gross) is used more than NDP — difficulty in accurately measuring depreciation across sectors
High depreciation rate → wider gap between Gross and Net aggregates → overstates productive capacity if only gross figures used

concepts.name: Personal Income, Disposable Income, and National Income: The Aggregates Ladder
key_dimensions: National Income (NNP at FC) → Personal Income (add transfers, subtract retained earnings, corporate taxes) → Personal Disposable Income (subtract personal taxes)
UPSC trap: National Income ≠ Personal Income — retained corporate profits and social security contributions are deducted
Per Capita Income as a welfare indicator — limitations (ignores distribution, ignores non-market activities)
Distinction between Personal Disposable Income and Private Final Consumption Expenditure

concepts.name: Underground Economy, Informal Sector, and GDP Underestimation in India
key_dimensions: Three categories excluded or poorly measured: illegal activities, informal/unorganized sector, non-monetized household production
UPSC trap: Household services (cooking, childcare at home) are NOT in GDP; if outsourced, they ARE — Hausman's feminist critique
India-specific: Over 50% of GDP may originate in informal sector — measured via NSSO surveys, not direct accounts
Demonetization 2016 and its impact on informal sector GDP measurement controversy

concepts.name: GDP and Welfare: Limitations as a Development Indicator
key_dimensions: GDP ignores income distribution (Gini coefficient), environmental degradation, and non-economic welfare
UPSC trap: Higher GDP growth with rising inequality may reduce median welfare — GDP per capita vs median income distinction
Alternatives: HDI, GNH (Bhutan), Green GDP/Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI), SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting)
Kuznets' own warning — GDP creator Simon Kuznets cautioned against using it as welfare measure

concepts.name: Advance Estimates, Revised Estimates, and GDP Data Architecture in India
key_dimensions: MoSPI releases: First Advance Estimate (Jan), Second Advance Estimate (Feb), First Revised Estimate (Jan next year), up to Third Revised Estimate
UPSC trap: Union Budget presented in February uses First Advance Estimate — based on only 7-8 months of data, subject to large revisions
Benchmark-indicator method used for advance estimates — relies on proxy indicators (IIP, tax data, corporate results)
Revision bias in India's GDP data — whether advance estimates systematically overestimate or underestimate final figures

concepts.name: Three Methods Equivalence: The GDP Identity and Why All Three Give the Same Answer
key_dimensions: Output Method = Income Method = Expenditure Method — the accounting identity ensures equivalence in theory
In practice, Statistical Discrepancy arises — how it is treated in India's national accounts
UPSC trap: The identity holds by definition, not by coincidence — every purchase is someone's income; every income comes from some output
Which method is primary in India (Output/GVA method) vs USA (Expenditure method) — and why

concepts.name: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) vs Market Exchange Rate for International GDP Comparison
key_dimensions: PPP adjusts for price level differences — reflects actual volume of goods/services, not currency values
UPSC trap: India's GDP rank by PPP (3rd globally) is much higher than by nominal USD (5th/6th) — PPP favors countries with low price levels
Balassa-Samuelson Effect: Non-traded services are cheaper in developing countries → PPP GDP > Nominal GDP for developing nations
IMF/World Bank use PPP for welfare comparisons; nominal GDP used for trade, debt sustainability, and financial comparisons
